subject: Agriculture
title: Peanuts and Groundnuts
description: Learn Peanuts and Groundnuts in one minute.

hook.text: Peanuts aren't nuts—they're legumes that bury their fruit underground. They fix nitrogen while producing food.

buildup.text: Originating in South America, peanuts spread globally via Portuguese and Spanish traders in the 1500s.

discovery.text: George Washington Carver promoted peanuts as a rotation crop to restore Southern US soils exhausted by cotton.

twist.text: Peanut allergies affect 2% of Western children and are increasing—the reason is still debated by scientists.

climax.text: In Africa and South Asia, peanuts provide critical protein where meat is scarce—they're a survival crop.

punchline.text: It's not a nut. It grows underground. And it feeds hundreds of millions.

quiz.question: Why did George Washington Carver promote peanut farming?
options: As a rotation crop to restore soil nitrogen depleted by cotton

details.summary: Peanuts, also called groundnuts, are legumes that develop their pods underground. This topic covers peanut cultivation, their dual role as food and oilseed crop, and their importance for nutrition and income in tropical developing countries.
details.whyItMatters: Peanuts provide affordable protein and fat for hundreds of millions of people in developing nations. As a legume, they also fix nitrogen and improve soil fertility for following crops.
takeaways: Peanuts are legumes, not tree nuts, and they fix nitrogen like other legumes
China and India together produce over 50% of the world's peanut crop
Peanut-based therapeutic foods treat severe malnutrition in children worldwide

faq.question: Why are peanuts classified as legumes rather than nuts?
faq.answer: Peanuts belong to the legume family (Fabaceae) and develop in pods like beans and peas. They grow underground after the flower stalk bends down and pushes the developing pod into the soil, unlike tree nuts that grow above ground.

faq.question: How do peanuts contribute to global nutrition programs?
faq.answer: Ready-to-use therapeutic foods made from peanut paste provide high-calorie, nutrient-dense treatment for severe child malnutrition. Products like Plumpy'Nut have saved millions of lives in famine-affected regions.
